discovery: The titanium-sapphire laser and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and SESAM) that made robust femtosecond lasers possible
motivation: Modern ultrafast science stands on a handful of enabling inventions. Moulton's titanium-doped sapphire laser (1982-86) offered a uniquely broad gain bandwidth. Sibbett's 1991 discovery of self-mode-locking, explained as Kerr-lens mode-locking, made that bandwidth usable as clean, stable femtosecond pulses from a simple laser cavity. Keller's semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM) made passive mode-locking reliable and self-starting across many solid-state and fibre lasers. Together these advances turned femtosecond pulses from a fragile specialty into a routine tool. They are the oscillators behind chirped pulse amplification, attosecond physics, optical frequency combs, multiphoton microscopy, and ophthalmic and industrial micromachining. Several Nobel Prizes have depended on these sources, yet the sources themselves have never been recognised. This is instrumentation that opened entire fields of physics, biology and medicine, and it deserves the Prize.
